Elegant ggplot2 (First Steps), with tidyplots equivalents

Source: elegant_ggplot2_vs_tidyplot_2.qmd

Author

Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)

Published

2026-06-24 12:11

About this handout

This follows the First steps chapter of Hadley Wickham, Danielle Navarro, and Thomas Lin Pedersen’s ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis (3rd edition). For each step we keep the original ggplot2 code and plot, then add the tidyplots code that produces the same figure.

The two grammars in one line:

  • ggplot2 maps columns to aesthetics inside aes(), then stacks geom_*() and scale_*() layers with +.
  • tidyplots pipes the data frame in, then chains add_*(), adjust_*(), and remove_*() verbs with the native pipe |>.

This chapter is mostly scatterplots and distributions, so most steps map cleanly to a tidyplots verb. Two recurring frictions show up and are worth naming up front:

  1. No transformed expressions in mappings. ggplot2 happily takes aes(y = unemploy / pop) or colour = factor(cyl). tidyplots’ tidyplot() wants bare column names, so we precompute those columns with mutate() first.
  2. No native verb for a few geoms (frequency polygons, paths). For those we use the escape hatch add(ggplot2::...), which drops a raw ggplot2 layer into a tidyplot.

Setup

library(ggplot2)        # the book's package
library(tidyplots)      # the package we translate each step into
library(dplyr)          # for the mutate()/filter() precompute steps
library(mgcv)           # for the GAM smoother example
data("mpg", package = "ggplot2")          # 234 car models
data("economics", package = "ggplot2")    # US economic time series

The mpg data has one row per car model, with engine displacement (displ), highway mileage (hwy), city mileage (cty), drivetrain (drv), and class.

1. Key components: a basic scatterplot

Every plot needs data, an aesthetic mapping, and at least one geom. The mapping goes inside aes() in ggplot2 and inside tidyplot() in tidyplots. Points are geom_point() versus add_data_points().

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +   # data + x/y mapping
  geom_point()                           # draw points

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>        # data + x/y mapping
  add_data_points()                      # draw points

2. Colour, size, shape, and other aesthetic attributes

To map a variable to colour, put it in the mapping: ggplot2’s aes(colour = class) becomes tidyplots’ color = class inside tidyplot().

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point()

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points()

Mapped vs. fixed. A constant colour is not an aesthetic, it is a fixed argument. In ggplot2 it goes outside aes(), in tidyplots it goes as a plain argument to the geom verb. (Putting "blue" inside the mapping instead makes ggplot2 invent a one-level legend, the classic beginner trap.)

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(colour = "blue")   # fixed colour, no legend

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points(color = "blue")   # fixed colour, no legend

3. Faceting

facet_wrap(~ class) makes one panel per class. tidyplots’ native verb is split_plot(by = class), but there is a real difference to know about. facet_wrap() gives every panel the same x and y range, while split_plot() builds each panel as an independent plot and free-scales it, so every panel ends up with its own y axis and the panels are no longer directly comparable. To match ggplot2’s shared scales we use the escape hatch add(ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ class)), which keeps tidyplots’ styling but ggplot2’s faceting (and its shared scales).

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ class)

tidyplots

mpg |>
  # tidyplots defaults to a fixed absolute panel size (50 x 50 mm, hence its
  # stubborn 1:1 panels). width = NA, height = NA lets the panels flex to fill
  # the figure like ggplot2, which is what makes faceting share scales cleanly.
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  # split_plot(by = class) free-scales each panel; the escape hatch facet_wrap
  # keeps ggplot2's shared x and y scales so panels are comparable.
  add(ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ class))

4. Plot geoms

4.1 Adding a smoother

geom_smooth() adds a fitted curve with a confidence band. tidyplots wraps the same machinery in add_curve_fit(). Both default to a loess fit. Extra arguments (se, span, method, formula) pass straight through in both.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()           # loess by default, with a ribbon

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  add_curve_fit()         # loess by default, with a ribbon

Controlling the wiggliness. span sets how local the loess fit is (smaller is wigglier). It passes through add_curve_fit() unchanged.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(span = 0.2)   # very local, wiggly

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  add_curve_fit(span = 0.2)

Other models. A GAM and a straight line are just different method= (and for the GAM, a formula=). Identical arguments in both packages.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x))

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  add_curve_fit(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x))

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points() |>
  add_curve_fit(method = "lm")

4.2 Boxplots and jittered points

With a discrete x, raw points overplot badly. Three fixes: jitter, boxplot, violin. tidyplots has a verb for each.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy)) +
  geom_point()   # heavy overplotting at three x positions

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points()

Jitter. geom_jitter() becomes add_data_points_jitter().

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy)) + geom_jitter()

tidyplots

# add_data_points_jitter() defaults to jitter_width = 0.2 (the full spread).
# geom_jitter()'s default width = 0.4 is a half-width (points displaced +/- 0.4),
# so the full ggplot2 spread is ~0.8; set jitter_width = 0.8 to match.
mpg |> tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points_jitter(jitter_width = 0.8)

Boxplot. geom_boxplot() becomes add_boxplot().

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy)) + geom_boxplot()

tidyplots

mpg |> tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |> add_boxplot()

Violin. geom_violin() becomes add_violin().

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy)) + geom_violin()

tidyplots

mpg |> tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |> add_violin()

4.3 Histograms and frequency polygons

A single continuous variable. geom_histogram() maps to add_histogram(). tidyplots has no frequency-polygon verb, so geom_freqpoly() uses the escape hatch.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) + geom_histogram()

tidyplots

mpg |> tidyplot(x = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |> add_histogram()

Frequency polygon (escape hatch).

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 2.5)

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add(ggplot2::geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 2.5))   # no native freqpoly verb

Comparing distributions across a subgroup. Map drv to colour for the frequency polygon, or to fill plus a facet for the histogram. In tidyplots the grouping aesthetic is always color, which maps to the fill for a histogram.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, colour = drv)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 0.5)

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = displ, color = drv, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add(ggplot2::geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 0.5))

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, fill = drv)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ drv, ncol = 1)

tidyplots

mpg |>
  # width = NA, height = NA frees tidyplots' fixed 1:1 panel size so the three
  # stacked panels flex to fill the figure (no clipped bottom panel).
  tidyplot(x = displ, color = drv, width = NA, height = NA) |>   # color = fill
  add_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) |>
  # split_plot(by = drv) free-scales each panel's y axis; the escape hatch
  # facet_wrap keeps ggplot2's shared y scale so panel heights are comparable.
  add(ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ drv, ncol = 1))

4.4 Bar charts

Two distinct cases. With raw data, geom_bar() counts rows per category, which is add_count_bar() in tidyplots.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(manufacturer)) + geom_bar()

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = manufacturer, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_count_bar()

With data already summarized, ggplot2 needs stat = "identity" to plot the value as is. tidyplots names that intent directly: add_sum_bar() draws the (single) value per category.

ggplot2

drugs <- data.frame(drug = c("a", "b", "c"), effect = c(4.2, 9.7, 6.1))
ggplot(drugs, aes(drug, effect)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")

tidyplots

drugs |>
  tidyplot(x = drug, y = effect, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_sum_bar()   # one value per group, plotted as is

4.5 Time series: line and path

Lines join points in x order, paths join them in data order. geom_line() maps to add_line(). geom_path() has no native verb, so it uses the escape hatch.

Note the transformed y, unemploy / pop. ggplot2 computes it inside aes(), but tidyplots needs a real column, so we mutate() it first.

ggplot2

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line()

tidyplots

economics |>
  mutate(unemploy_rate = unemploy / pop) |>   # precompute, no aes() math
  tidyplot(x = date, y = unemploy_rate, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_line()

Path coloured by year. Both the y ratio and the year(date) colour are transformed, so both become precomputed columns for tidyplots. The path itself is the escape hatch, drawn uncoloured, then the coloured points go on top.

ggplot2

year <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$year + 1900
ggplot(economics, aes(unemploy / pop, uempmed)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = year(date)))

tidyplots

economics |>
  mutate(unemploy_rate = unemploy / pop,
         year = as.POSIXlt(date)$year + 1900) |>
  tidyplot(x = unemploy_rate, y = uempmed, color = year, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add(ggplot2::geom_path(ggplot2::aes(color = NULL), colour = "grey50")) |>
  add_data_points()

5. Modifying the axes

Axis titles. xlab()/ylab() become adjust_x_axis_title()/ adjust_y_axis_title(), and dropping a title is a remove_*_axis_title() verb rather than passing NULL. The semi-transparent points use a fixed alpha in both.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1 / 3) +
  xlab("city driving (mpg)") +
  ylab("highway driving (mpg)")

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = cty, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points(alpha = 1 / 3) |>
  adjust_x_axis_title("city driving (mpg)") |>
  adjust_y_axis_title("highway driving (mpg)")

Removing the titles.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1 / 3) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)

tidyplots

mpg |>
  tidyplot(x = cty, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points(alpha = 1 / 3) |>
  remove_x_axis_title() |>
  remove_y_axis_title()

Axis limits. Continuous limits are ylim(20, 30) versus adjust_y_axis(limits = c(20, 30)). Selecting which categories of a discrete axis to keep is xlim("f", "r") in ggplot2, but tidyplots has no category-picking limit, so we filter the data instead.

ggplot2

ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25) +
  xlim("f", "r") +     # keep only front- and rear-wheel drive
  ylim(20, 30)         # clip y to 20..30

tidyplots

mpg |>
  dplyr::filter(drv %in% c("f", "r")) |>   # the category pick, done as a filter
  tidyplot(x = drv, y = hwy, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points_jitter() |>
  adjust_y_axis(limits = c(20, 30))

6. Output

Both packages return an object you can store, print, and save. tidyplots returns a ggplot under the hood, so ggsave() still works, but tidyplots also ships its own save_plot() (note the argument order: the plot comes first).

# build and store
p <- mpg |>
  mutate(cyl_f = factor(cyl)) |>           # factor(cyl) precomputed for tidyplots
  tidyplot(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cyl_f, width = NA, height = NA) |>
  add_data_points()

p                                          # print it

save_plot(p, "plot.png", width = 10, height = 10, units = "cm")   # tidyplots
ggplot2::ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 5, height = 5)             # also works

Takeaways

  • For the everyday plots in this chapter, tidyplots has a one-to-one verb: add_data_points(), add_curve_fit(), add_boxplot(), add_violin(), add_histogram(), add_count_bar(), add_line().
  • The grammar difference is where the mapping lives: inside aes() for ggplot2, inside tidyplot() for tidyplots, with grouping always carried by color.
  • Two things force you off the happy path. tidyplots will not evaluate transformed expressions in a mapping (so precompute with mutate()), and it has no verb for a handful of geoms like geom_freqpoly() and geom_path() (so reach for the escape hatch add(ggplot2::...)).
  • split_plot() is tidyplots’ faceting verb, but it free-scales each panel. Use add(ggplot2::facet_wrap(...)) when you need ggplot2’s shared scales.

References

  • Wickham H, Navarro D, Pedersen TL. ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis (3rd edition). The source for this handout (chapter First steps). https://ggplot2-book.org/getting-started.html
  • Engler JB (2025). “Tidyplots empowers life scientists with easy code-based data visualization.” iMeta, e70018. doi:10.1002/imt2.70018
  • Wood SN (2011). “Fast stable restricted maximum likelihood and marginal likelihood estimation of semiparametric generalized linear models.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society (B) 73(1):3-36. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2010.00749.x (the mgcv GAM smoother used in the smoother section).
